Welcome toTwo Dishes, One Receiver

Two radio dishes feed one receiver: how does its power change as a source drifts overhead?

About: a two-dish radio interferometer: how the mean power at one receiver depends on the direction of a distant source

About this simulation

On screen
Above: the two dishes on a horizontal scale from −30 m to 230 m, the cables to the receiver box, which glows in proportion to the mean power, and the parallel rays from the source at θ to the vertical (the angle drawn twenty times larger than it is). The dashed wavefront is at right angles to the rays through the dish the wave reaches first; the accent stretch on the other ray is the extra path ℓ sin θ. Below: the mean power as a fraction of its value overhead against θ from −120′ to +120′, with the single-dish response dashed, the trace so far in the accent colour, the previous trace in grey and a bar the size of the Moon (31′).
Controls
Baseline ℓ, 30 to 200 m, and dish diameter D, 10 to 25 m: changing either stops the drift, turns the trace so far grey and keeps θ. The source angle θ, −120′ to +120′ in steps of 0.1′, with a box and preset buttons to land on an exact angle: moving it stops the drift. ▶ Drift carries the source at 6′ of arc per second until θ = +120′; ■ Stop drift halts it.
Measured
θ in minutes of arc; the extra path ℓ sin θ in wavelengths of λ = 21 cm; P/P0 the mean power over its value for a source overhead (single-dish response × two-dish fringe factor); 'one dish alone' the single-dish (Airy) response at the same θ. They appear in the Readouts panel in the sidebar.
Simplifications
One monochromatic point source at λ = 21 cm; both dishes point straight up and their signals are added in phase at the receiver (an adding interferometer). A real receiver has a finite bandwidth and real sources have a finite size, and both reduce the depth of the fringes. The drift is 24 times faster than the real sidereal drift of a source on the celestial equator, 15′ per minute.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A source drifting across

Keep the baseline at 100 m, the dish diameter at 25 m and the source at θ = −120′. Before pressing Drift, predict how the mean power at the receiver changes as the source drifts from −120′ to +120′. Then press Drift and watch the glow and the graph.

2 · The first zero

Keep the baseline at 100 m and the dish diameter at 25 m, and set θ to 0. You will raise θ slowly, watching the readout of the extra path in wavelengths. Before you do, predict the extra path at which the mean power first falls to zero.

3 · A longer baseline

Keep the dish diameter at 25 m and change the baseline from 100 m to 200 m, which turns the old trace grey. Before setting θ to −120′ and pressing Drift again, predict how the new trace compares with the old one.

4 · Smaller dishes

Keep the baseline at 200 m and change the dish diameter from 25 m to 12.5 m, which turns the old trace grey. Before setting θ to −120′ and pressing Drift again, predict how the new trace compares with the old one.

5 · A small shift off centre

Set the baseline to 200 m and the dish diameter to 25 m, and set θ to 0. You will move the source to θ = 2.0′, watching the last two readouts. Before you do, predict what happens to the mean power at the receiver and to the response of a single dish.

6 · What this shows

Two dishes a baseline ℓ apart turn the smooth response of one dish into fringes. The extra path ℓ sin θ changes by a whole wavelength every λ/ℓ, so the power at the receiver swings between full and zero on that angular scale, inside each dish's broad hump, about λ/D wide. The spacing depends only on ℓ, so a long baseline locates a source to about λ/ℓ, far finer than one dish's λ/D: this is why radio telescopes are built as arrays.

The Physics

A Radio Interferometer of Two Dishes · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A radio source drifts across the sky above two dishes. Their signals are added at one receiver, and the sim plots the mean power at the receiver against the angle of the source.

What you'll learn

  • What extra path the wave travels to reach the second dish.
  • What the receiver measures as the source drifts.
  • What the baseline sets, and what the dish diameter sets.
  • Why radio telescopes are built as arrays of dishes.
The set-up, as the sim draws it: two dishes a baseline ℓ apart, cables of equal length to one receiver, and parallel rays from a source at angle θ to the vertical. The sim draws the angle of the rays 20 times larger than it is.

What's on screen

  • Dashed line: the wavefront, at right angles to the rays, through the dish the wave reaches first.
  • Bright stretch of the other ray: the extra path ℓ sin θ.
  • Receiver: its glow grows with the mean power.
  • Bright trace in the graph below: P/P0 against θ, so far.
  • Dashed curve: the response of one dish alone.
  • Grey trace: the previous trace, kept when you change ℓ or D.
  • Bar: the Moon, 31′ across, for scale.
See itLook at the opening arrangement. Watch for: the two dishes and the receiver, the rays arriving at an angle, the dashed wavefront, and the graph still empty.

03

The extra path: the wave reaches one dish later

Let a distant source lie at angle θ to the vertical, in the plane that holds the baseline (the notes' Figure 8). Its wave arrives as a plane wave, so the wavefront is a straight line at right angles to the rays. Draw it through the dish the wave reaches first. The wave still has to travel from the wavefront to the other dish. That distance is the short side of a right triangle whose long side is the baseline:

The triangle behind the bright stretch in the sim. The angle at dish 1 is θ, the same as between the rays and the vertical.
The extra path, and the time Δt by which the second dish hears the wave later. c is the speed of light.

The sim keeps sin θ, and reads the path in wavelengths of the 21 cm line, λ = 0.21 m. At ℓ = 100 m a source at θ = 20′ gives ℓ sin θ = 0.58 m, which is 2.77 λ. The sim draws the angle of the rays 20 times larger than it is, so the path can be seen.

Cables of equal length bring both signals to one receiver. The extra path is therefore the only difference between them.

Key idea. The two dishes receive the same wave, but one of them hears it ℓ sin θ later.
See itMove the source to θ = +20′. Watch for: the bright stretch on the second ray, and the extra path reading 2.77 λ.
04

Fringes: the power swings with the extra path

For radiation of one frequency ν, the voltages from the two receivers are, in the notes' equation (1.23):

Va is their common amplitude.

The receiver adds them and measures the mean of (V1 + V2)2. The squares each average to Va2/2. In the cross term, one cosine averages to zero and the other survives, with νΔt = ℓ sin θ/λ:

Equation (1.24). The sim divides by the value for a source overhead, where it is 2Va2.

This factor is 1 wherever ℓ sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths. These maxima are the fringes, as in Young's two-slit experiment with the dishes in place of the slits. It is 0 where the extra path is half a wavelength, and again at every further whole step. Near the vertical, sin θ ≈ θ, so neighbouring fringes are separated by λ/ℓ: 7.2′ at ℓ = 100 m, with the first zero halfway, at 3.6′.

The fringe factor alone, at ℓ = 100 m, from the same functions as the sim.
Key idea. The fringe spacing λ/ℓ depends on the baseline alone.
See itGo to θ = +3.6′, then to +7.2′. Watch for: the extra path reading 0.50 λ with the power close to zero, then the path reading 1.00 λ with a fringe at its top.
05

The hump: one dish alone responds broadly

Each dish has its own response to the direction of the source. For a circular dish of diameter D, the sim uses the Airy pattern, 2J1(x)/x, squared, with x = πD sin θ/λ. It is 1 at θ = 0 and falls to zero first at 1.22λ/D, the diffraction limit of the notes: 35.2′ for D = 25 m. The notes give its width as of order λ/D. This is the dashed curve, and the sim's "one dish alone" readout.

Both dishes have the same response. The power at the receiver, as a fraction of its value overhead, is the product of the two factors:

The sim's P/P0. The cosine squared is the fringe factor, and the bracket is one dish alone.
P/P0 at ℓ = 100 m and D = 25 m, the notes' Figure 8b. The fringes lie within the response of a single dish.

The fringes are narrow because λ/ℓ is small. The hump is broad because λ/D is larger, since the baseline is longer than a dish is wide. At ℓ = 100 m and D = 25 m there are nine fringe maxima inside the central hump. Their heights follow it: 1.00 at θ = 0, 0.86 at the first fringe, 0.52 at the second.

Key idea. The receiver's power is a narrow fringe pattern, shaped by the broad response of one dish.
See itDrift the source from −50′ to +50′. Watch for: the power rising and falling through a run of fringes, their tops following the dashed curve of one dish alone.
06

Baseline and dish: each sets its own scale

The two factors depend on different lengths. The fringe factor contains ℓ, so its spacing λ/ℓ depends only on the baseline. The one-dish response contains D, so the position 1.22λ/D of its first zero depends only on the dish.

ℓDFringe spacing λ/ℓHump, first zeroFringe maxima in the hump
100 m25 m7.2′±35.2′9
200 m25 m3.6′±35.2′19
200 m12.5 m3.6′±70.4′39
The three rows of the table, from the sim's functions. Dashed: one dish alone.

Doubling ℓ halves the fringe spacing and leaves the hump alone. Halving D doubles the width of the hump and leaves the spacing alone, so the hump holds about twice as many fringes. Smaller dishes do not blur the fringes. They only widen the hump. The sim plots power as a fraction of its value overhead, so the smaller collecting area of a small dish does not show.

Key idea. The baseline sets the fringes. The dish sets the hump they sit in.
See itDouble the baseline, from ℓ = 100 m to 200 m. Watch for: the old trace turning grey, and the new fringes half as far apart inside a hump of the same width.
See itHalve the dish, from D = 25 m to 12.5 m, at ℓ = 200 m. Watch for: the old trace turning grey, and the new trace keeping its fringe spacing inside a hump twice as wide.
07

Arrays: the baseline does the locating

One dish locates a source only to about 1.22λ/D. The notes' example is a dish 100 m across at 21 cm: about ten minutes of arc, a third of the Moon (the formula gives 8.8′). Two dishes do better, because the source moves through the fringes as the Earth turns, and the times at which it crosses them fix its position to a small fraction of λ/ℓ. A baseline can be far longer than any dish is wide.

Angles at 21 cm. The fringe spacing λ/ℓ is a small fraction of 1.22λ/D for the 25 m dish of the sim.

A small shift shows it. At ℓ = 200 m, move the source from θ = 0 to 2.0′. The extra path becomes 0.554 λ, and the fringe factor falls to cos2(π × 0.554) = 0.029, so P/P0 = 0.028. One 25 m dish has barely noticed: its response is still 0.99, because 2.0′ is 18 times smaller than its first zero. The notes' Problem 4 adds that away from the vertical the fringes are λ/(ℓ cos θ1) apart, where ℓ cos θ1 is the baseline seen from the source.

Key idea. A longer baseline locates a source more finely, whatever the size of the dishes.
See itAt ℓ = 200 m, move the source from θ = 0 to +2.0′. Watch for: the extra path reading 0.55 λ, the power falling to 0.03, and the response of one dish alone staying near 0.99.
08

Where it matters: arrays and very long baselines

An array of many dishes has many baselines, of different lengths and directions. As the Earth rotates, each baseline turns relative to the source. Combining the signals of all the pairs over many hours builds up an image as sharp as that of a single dish as large as the array. This is aperture synthesis, for which Ryle received the Nobel Prize in 1974.

In very-long-baseline interferometry the dishes are on different continents. Each records its signal together with the time from an atomic clock, and the recordings are combined afterwards. With baselines as long as the diameter of the Earth, and wavelengths of a few centimetres or less, the resolution is better than a thousandth of a second of arc. At 3 cm and 12 700 km, λ/ℓ is 0.5 milliarcseconds.

The sim uses one monochromatic point source and adds the two signals in phase, an adding interferometer. A real receiver has a finite bandwidth, and real sources have a finite size. Both reduce the depth of the fringes.

09

Summary

In one line. Two dishes add the signals from one source, and the mean power at their receiver depends on the baseline, on the dish diameter and on the angle of the source.

Common mix-ups

  • "The power rises once, to the hump of a single dish." It rises and falls through many fringes inside the hump: nine at ℓ = 100 m and D = 25 m.
  • "The first zero comes after a whole wavelength of extra path." It comes after half a wavelength: at 3.6′ for ℓ = 100 m.
  • "A longer baseline widens everything." It halves the fringe spacing and leaves the hump where it was.
  • "Smaller dishes blur the fringes." The fringes keep their spacing. The hump becomes wider.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ℓ = 30 m, D = 25 m and θ = 24.1′. The path should read 1.00 λ, and P/P0 should equal the dish alone, 0.13.
  • Set ℓ = 100 m and θ = +20′. The path should read 2.77 λ, and P/P0 about 0.15.
